text: Tories welcome Haigh's hint government could adopt their plan to scrap Natural England
Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos.
In a story in the Times today, Patrick Maguire says:

double quotation markThe Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs. Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the construction of infrastructure.

Asked about this report, Haigh told Sky News this morning that the government did want to reduce the number of quangos – and she declined to say whether or not this would include Natural England. She said:

double quotation markWe’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.

At their party conference, the Conservatives proposed abolishing Natural England and the Environment Agency. In a move the party may now regret, Labour issued a response suggesting there was no need for this because the government was making both quangos more effective.
Today Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, said:

double quotation markFor far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure. That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale. I don’t know who they think they’re kidding: this is a government that has spent two years piling on ever more bureaucracy. Only the Conservatives will take on the anti-growth ideologues and build the homes and infrastructure Britain needs.
CBI chief Rain Newton-Smith welcomes Burnham's debate on closer relations with EU, saying 'Brexit was wrong turn'
Rain Newton-Smith, the CBI chief executive, opened the organisation’s conference in London this morning with some relatively positive comments about the PM. Here are extracts from what she said.
Newton-Smith praised Burnham for bringing “hope” back to politics. She said:

double quotation markIn the last few years, we in the UK have been too ready to talk ourselves down. To put on our gloom-tinted glasses. They don’t sit well on me. The prime minister has brought a dose of hope to our politics. And just as pessimism can be self-fulfilling, confidence can be contagious. It’s time we gave a shot of confidence to our economy. It’s time we got serious about a brighter future for our children.
She said the government needed to reassure business that “public control” of utilities did not mean nationalisation.

double quotation markOn investment … to some, “public control” sounds like code for renationalisation. That is kryptonite to investment. We know that’s not what’s coming – but give us the reassurance we need. Show this is a model built on partnership, not primacy. That government wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit.
The government has heard this message. See 9.15am.
She said Burnham was right to start a debate about a closer relationship with the EU.

double quotation markThe prime minister is right to have this conversation. Brexit was a wrong turn for our economy. It gave us greater sovereignty. But sovereignty without prosperity is not enough. We didn’t vote to be poorer. This is no time to re-fight the referendum. But we must come back to the table with bolder ambition.
She said that regional devolution could unlock investment and that the CBI was involved in a scheme to help give mayoral authorities more financial expertise.

double quotation markThere is promise in devolution. Done right, it can give business one front door for decisions that unlock investment. Done wrong, it could fracture confidence… leave regions competing with each other when they should be competing with the world. The difference is whether authorities have the capacity and skills. Today, I can announce the CBI and our members are partnering with the National Wealth Fund and mayoral authorities across the UK … to parachute in senior financial secondees with the experience to make investment happen.
Burnham to give update to MPs on UK-EU summit, as Haigh tells CBI plans for more public control of utilities 'not anti-business'

Good morning. This afternoon Andy Burnham will make a statement to MPs about the UK-EU summit on Friday, where agreements were reached on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. At one point there were suggestions that he might use this Commons moment to give a speech with further details of his plan for a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU, including possibly rejoin. Now, that won’t happen today; Burnham has decided to make that announcement part of his 10-year plan, which is being unveiled next month. But dozens of MPs will get the chance to put a question to Burnham, and so we will get a sense of what they feel about the prospect of revisiting the Brexit settlement.
According to the BBC, Burnham will describe the Friday deal as “the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament”.
He will tell parliament on Monday the “landmark” deal struck with the EU means there is a “very real prospect” the next decade can be “much better” than the last one.

We will hear alternative views at the CBI conference today. All the main UK opposition party leaders are speaking, and Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, are planning to criticise the agreement with Brussels, according to extracts of their remarks released overnight.

Burnham won’t be there himself. But he is sending his de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, and she is planning to reassure the CBI audience that Burnham’s plan for more public control of utilities does not mean the government is anti-business.

double quotation markThis government will put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology. Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.
She will point out that foreign governments already own “significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks with returns paid to their taxpayers” and she will say:
double quotation markThe status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.
In its overnight briefing on the speech, the Cabinet Office says:

double quotation markChallenging the misconception that public control means wholesale nationalisation, the first secretary will say this approach is not about whether or not markets work, but how effective monopolies have resulted in a lack of genuine competition.
Here is the agenda for the day.

9.30am: Rain Newton-Smith, the CBI chief executive, opens the annual CBI conference with a speech. There are also speeches from Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, at 9.45am and Kemi Badenoch at 12.20pm, and Q&A events with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, at 2.35pm, Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, at 3.55pm and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, at 4.40pm.
Morning: Andy Burnham is due to visit a Morrisons in Kent to promote claims his SPS deal with the EU will help keep down food prices.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Burnham is expected to make a statement to the Commons about Friday’s UK-EU summit.
